body_markdown:
*John* writes:


Dear Sajeev,


I read the[Hagerty news piece](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/nhtsa-updates-headlight-regulations-adaptive-headlights/) about NHTSA reviewing and updating its headlight regulations. It seems like something to be excited about—if done right, it could lead to a real change in how the front end of cars are designed and stop new cars from blinding us by more intelligently aiming the lights. The downside to allowing new tech and “intelligent” lighting is added expense—and replacement lights for new cars are already stratospherically expensive, and costly parts lead to higher insurance premiums.


So what say you? Given that you have one foot in design and the other in practical knowledge, you seem like the right person to ask.


*Sajeev* answers:


I am generally excited about this news, mostly because these smart, “matrix headlights” are now a one-size-fits-all affair for a much larger part of the world. Tesla has these matrices for U.S. customers, but now imported brands can apply their technology to our market without needing to reinvent the wheel just to appease our (likely outdated and flawed) regulations.


The big benefit for the consumer is that more brands can use the same headlight, theoretically lowering their replacement cost. Even if the OEM headlight is costly, perhaps the aftermarket can now reproduce it with the justification of a quicker return on its investment.


Heck, we might even see cheaper cars adopt the technology, if it can be simplified and available as a bolt-in assembly easily integrated into an automaker’s product portfolio. Maybe I am a bit too bullish on this news, but we likely have reasons to celebrate.


That’s because European designs were better even in the days of sealed-beam headlights. The average Hella H4 headlight assembly had a crisper cutoff, with a beam that kicked out to the side to illuminate road signs. The American headlight beam was closer to a shotgun, and the situation has only gotten worse with all the illegal, aftermarket junk we see online these days.


It would be nice to get these European “E-code” headlights in America and use them legally.[NHTSA’s press release](https://landline.media/nhtsa-looks-to-dim-headlight-glare/#:~:text=Aligning%20global%20standards) was vague when it said the organization is “aligning global standards” and “streamlining test procedures for plastic optics and replaceable lenses.” What does that mean, practically?


LED chips done right: standard H4 Halogen (left) and Osram H4 LED (right)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I am hoping this news means Americans can get[ECE/E-code lights from the EU](https://agri-lighting.co.uk/tractor-lighting/safety/e-mark-approval-explained/#:~:text=Each%20contracting%20party%20has%20a%20fixed%20number.%20These%20are%20the%20codes%20you%20are%20most%20likely%20to%20see%20on%20lighting%20sold%20in%20the%20UK%3A) with less friction. Because that would suggest we could legally purchase something like the Osram Nightbreaker LED (which[can be road-legal](https://www.osram.de/am/night-breaker-led/night-breaker-led-ledcheck.jsp?mkt=/ledcheck/) in Europe) and pop it into a Hella headlight assembly. I have sampled the aforementioned Osram Nightbreaker and Hella E-code combination during the same month I tried out a new, 2024 Escalade with an LED array. They were shockingly similar in the quality of their light output and their inability to blind oncoming traffic on their low beam.


Don’t take what I read between the lines of a NHTSA press release as a promise that ECE lights will be legal and readily available for our older cars. But companies like Hella, Valeo, and Cibié might have reason to push their wares harder in America. Just like fancy matrix eyes on a new Audi, the appeal of more customers with little to no changes in your inventory sounds hard to resist.


Money is a huge motivator. So I look forward to more European-compliant headlights on our roads, be it on expensive new cars or classics with sealed beams.
